metadata.title: Why Partial JSON Can Be a Valid Object Before the Closing Brace Arrives
metadata.purpose: Take apart what the Anthropic TypeScript SDK's streaming parser actually does — a stack that closes every open structure with a zero-value default the instant a chunk ends. Name the design choice: usable-and-provisional over correct-and-late. Land the carry-out that shape-safe and value-final are two different guarantees, and the parser only gives you the first.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B04 (four-chunk {"q": "solar case, paid off by splitting each snapshot into shape-safe vs. value-still-growing)

beats.narration_text: A half-finished JSON string, no brace yet — a normal parser throws on it. Anthropic's SDK hands back a usable object after every chunk. So how does a partial string already parse?

beats.narration_text: Standard JSON.parse is unforgiving by design — it demands a complete document, brace to brace. Feed it a half-finished string and it throws, no partial credit. So the reasonable guess is that a streaming snapshot behaves the same way: broken until the brace lands, error if you read it early. That guess is wrong. The streaming parser was built with a different priority.

shot.new_visual_element: A half-finished string splitting into a THROWS path (standard parser) and a question-marked path (streaming snapshot)

production_viz.label: Two paths, one unresolved
production_viz.mechanic: A card labelled 'HALF-FINISHED STRING' on cream, feeding two arrows. Top arrow to a card labelled 'JSON.parse' which throws (crossed with terracotta X, captioned 'THROWS'). Bottom arrow to a card labelled '.on(inputJson)' with a large question mark, captioned 'streaming snapshot — ?'.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. A search tool streams the argument `{"q": "solar` across four chunks. Each chunk fires `.on('inputJson')`, and each fire hands back a `jsonSnapshot`: `{}`, then `{"q":""}`, then `{"q":"sol"}`, then `{"q":"solar"}`. Four snapshots, four parseable objects — before the real closing brace has arrived at all.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - four snapshots ticking across a timeline, each stamped VALID

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - four snapshots, each already valid
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A horizontal timeline with four tick marks. At each tick, a small card appears in sequence: '{}', then '{"q":""}', then '{"q":"sol"}', then '{"q":"solar"}' (monospace, terracotta border). Each card gets a terracotta VALID stamp the instant it appears. Header reads 'search_database streams {"q": "solar'. THIS FOUR-CARD TIMELINE COMPOSITION RETURNS AT B04.

beats.narration_text: Here's the machinery. The parser keeps a stack of every object and array it has opened. The instant a chunk ends, it walks that stack and closes each open structure with a zero-value default — empty string, empty object. Nothing waits for the real closing brace; the parser supplies its own. They optimized for feedback speed at the cost of ever handing you a value you can trust as final.

shot.new_visual_element: A token stream feeding a stack; the stack sealing shut into a complete tree at each cut point

production_viz.label: The stack seals itself shut
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a token stream ('{', '"q"', ':', '"sol') feeding into a vertical stack of open-structure markers ('{ open', 'string open'). Right: at a cut point (dashed terracotta line), the stack markers each sprout a closing counterpart ('}' , '"') labelled 'zero-value default', producing a complete tree diagram, captioned 'no real closing brace here'.

beats.narration_text: So back to the search call: `{}` isn't an empty query — it's a query string that hasn't started arriving yet. And `{"q":"sol"}` isn't the final query — three more characters are still on the wire. That's the trade the design makes: a snapshot tells you the shape is safe to read, but says nothing about whether the value inside has stopped changing. Shape-safe and value-final are two different guarantees, and the parser only gives you the first.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - the same four snapshots, now each split into shape: safe and value: still growing

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - shape-safe vs. value-still-growing
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 TIMELINE COMPOSITION RETURNS: the same four snapshot cards ('{}', '{"q":""}', '{"q":"sol"}', '{"q":"solar"}') now each split by a horizontal divider into two labels: top 'SHAPE: SAFE' (ink), bottom 'VALUE: STILL GROWING' (terracotta) — except the final card, whose bottom label reads 'VALUE: DONE' in ink (no accent — it is not the thing still changing).

beats.narration_text: The parser closes every open structure for you. A valid snapshot tells you the shape is safe to read — not that the values inside are done.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt — paste it into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I'm streaming a tool call with the Anthropic TypeScript SDK and I see partial JSON arriving via the inputJson event. Walk me through why each chunk's jsonSnapshot is already a valid JS object before the closing brace arrives, and show me how to read a field from it safely mid-stream without waiting for the tool_use_delta done event. Go deeper: when a value inside a valid snapshot is a partially-streamed string or a truncated number, how is the parser defaulting it — and can you construct a case where the shape is safe but a naive read of the value is silently wrong? Liam, in for Bear.
